transcript: Motion carries. Thank you. Item number 12, please. Item 12, Communication from Councilwoman Price. Councilwoman Gonzalez. Councilman Austin. And Vice Mayor Richardson. Recommendation to develop develop an outreach and education campaign regarding youth marijuana use and drug impaired driving. Councilwoman Price. Thank you, Mr. Vice Mayor. So I want to first thank my colleagues for signing on to this item with me. I believe this is a very important item because it's not going to allow the city to be very proactive in establishing some best practices moving forward. And I think it gives the city of Long Beach an opportunity to be a leader in the region in terms of partnership and collaboration between policymakers, law enforcement and leaders in the marijuana dispensary businesses. When we look at some of the outreach and education components that we've seen in other industries, let's say with alcohol, we see that a lot of the major manufacturers and and bars and places where alcohol is served have partnered in this concept of outreach and education by sharing messages, encouraging people to drink responsibly, being aware and mindful collectively that there are negative consequences associated with misuse of certain products and really coming together to come up with outreach and education that addresses those issues. So I think where we are with with marijuana, especially in the state of California and in the city of Long Beach, is is very much in its infancy stage in terms of outreach and education, in fact, at a statewide level. There are requirements with the passage of Prop 64 that there be outreach that come directed from the state in regards to requirements for the industry to have warnings for the youth and things of that nature that are contained in the health and safety code. And so those changes are coming. But to my knowledge, there have been no local jurisdictions, no municipalities that have taken a proactive approach to the issue of outreach and education. And that's the intent behind this item. The item isn't to be intrusive or force anyone to do anything. It's really an opportunity to extend the olive branch and say, can we work together to meet our common goals? And I say that with with full understanding and fully admitting that I have had and continue to have some concerns regarding the impact, if any, that rolling out this industry will have on our existing city resources, our ability to enforce license, etc.. Those remain concerns of mine. Having said that, I fully respect and appreciate the outcome of an election. And in fact, when residents have called me in the last weeks to say, is there going to be a dispensary on my street? As I've heard what I say to them, as this is what was voted into law. And I think we all need to be mindful that our new reality is one that came about as a result of the vote of the people. And I fully respect that. I think when there are differences of opinion on controversial issues, it's very, very important. And I make it my personal mission to try to find areas of commonality. And one thing I have found in studying this particular industry is that the owners of the businesses, the folks that are legitimate business owners who are attempting to operate within the law, understand, respect and appreciate the goals of being proactive when it comes to drug impaired driving education and youth access. I think those individuals have shared with me repeatedly that they want to partner with the city in those efforts and in those endeavors and from the states that have participated in legislation that has decriminalized marijuana, Washington and Colorado. In my conversations with law enforcement officials in those states and staff who works for the Department of Transportation in those states. One of the things that I've been told repeatedly is that the one lesson that they learned that they wish they would have done differently is come to the table earlier with the marijuana industry to establish best practices. One example is that, you know, the state of Colorado, the Department of Transportation, came up with a series of public service announcements and they started broadcasting them, and they did so without coming to the table with the other stakeholders, namely the marijuana business owners. And one of the ads was found to be very offensive to users of marijuana. The portrayal and you can see it on YouTube, just marijuana, barbecue. Those are the keywords that you can type in to YouTube and you can see it. But there was a. Portrayal of a man attempting to, you know, basically fire up a barbecue under the influence of marijuana. And the gist of the PSA was, you know, trying to barbecue your food under the influence of marijuana is legal. Driving while under the influence of marijuana is not. And what happened with that ad is it was very funny, but the marijuana industry and the users found it to be very offensive. They felt that it portrayed the users in a very negative light. So the state actually had to pull back that ad and had wasted a lot of resources in creating the ad and marketing the ad. So my hope is that this is not one of those functions. There are several functions that the state has that are exclusive to the state. A regulatory functions that are exclusive to the state. Education and outreach in the area of marijuana use is not something that is. Limited to the state. Local jurisdictions can get involved in establishing best practices for the marijuana industry. And so the intent behind this item is for us to work with our health department. And I know that Kelly Collopy is here. I see her in the audience. I've talked with her quite a bit about this item. I think she understands the intent behind it, and I'm happy to answer any questions about the intent. But the intent is really to bring everybody to the table, make sure that everyone is on the same page in regards to the content of education and outreach for two simple objectives.
